column1: #SHEETINFO | name=Knowledge Base
What is Artificial Intelligence (AI)?
column2:
A broad field of computer science focused on creating machines that perform tasks typically requiring human intelligence, i.e. solving problems by simulating human behavior.

The term was coined in 1956.

column1: What is Machine Learning (ML)?
column2: A subset of AI in which models learn from data to perform a task, without being explicitly programmed, and improve over time.

column1: What is Generative AI?
column2:
Generative AI is a category of AI/ML systems that create new content (text, images, audio, video, code) rather than only analyzing, predicting or classifying existing data.

Modern implementations commonly use deep learning.

column1: What is Deep Learning?
column2: A specialized subset of ML that uses artificial neural networks with multiple layers to analyze complex data patterns.

column1: What is the nesting order of AI concepts?
column2: AI > Machine Learning > Deep Learning > Generative AI.

column1: What are the four primary ways to use gen AI?
column2:
* Create
* Summarize
* Discover
* Automate

column1: What is a foundation model?
column2:
A large, general-purpose model trained on massive, diverse (often multimodal) data that can be adapted to many downstream tasks.

Examples:
* Gemini
* GPT
* Claude
* Llama

column1: Why are they called "foundation" models?
column2: Because they serve as a baseline/foundation on which many different applications are built and consumed (via prompting, APIs, tuning).

column1: Traditional (predictive) AI model vs foundation model?
column2:
Traditional:
* Small specialist model built and trained in-house for one specific task (e.g. spam classifier).
Foundation:
* Generalist model trained on massive data, adaptable to many tasks.

column1: What is an LLM?
column2:
Large Language Model - a foundation model trained mostly on text.

Handles:
* Human languages
* Programming languages (e.g. Python).

column1: What is an LMM?
column2: Large Multimodal Model - a large model that handles multiple modalities (text, images, audio, video), the evolution of the LLM concept.

column1: What does "multimodal" mean?
column2:
A model/application that can ingest, process and generate multiple data types (modalities), such as:
* Text
* Images
* Audio
* Video
* PDFs

It means COMBINING types, not one specific type.

column1: What are diffusion models used for?
column2: Generating high-quality images, audio and video through iterative refinement of noise into content (e.g. photorealistic images from text descriptions).

column1: What is the Transformer?
column2:
A neural network architecture introduced in 2017 by Google engineers ("Attention Is All You Need").

The engine behind modern gen AI.

column1: What does GPT stand for?
column2: Generative Pre-trained Transformer.

column1: What type of data do neural networks accept as input?
column2:
Only numbers.

Non-numeric data (text, images) must first be converted to a numeric representation.

column1: What are embeddings?
column2:
Numeric vectors (lists of numbers) that represent the semantic meaning of text, images, etc.

Produced by an embedding model.

column1: What is a vector database?
column2:
A repository of embeddings (vectors) that enables semantic search.

In Google Cloud, AlloyDB, Spanner and BigQuery can be used for vector data.

column1: Semantic search vs keyword search?
column2:
Keyword search:
* Matches exact terms.
Semantic search:
* Matches by meaning/context (e.g. "run a marathon" vs "run for president").
RAG uses semantic search.

column1: What is a token?
column2:
The unit of processing/billing for foundation models: a piece of text (word or part of a word).
* Roughly 4 characters per token.
* ~100 tokens ≈ 75 English words.
* Varies by model and language.

column1: What is a context window?
column2:
The maximum amount of information (in tokens) a model can consider at one time - input plus output.

Differs by model.

column1: What is parametric memory?
column2:
What the model learned during training (stored in its parameters).

Without RAG/grounding, the model answers only from this plus the prompt.

column1: What is a knowledge cutoff?
column2:
The date after which the model has no training data.

It knows nothing published after it; use prompting, grounding or fine-tuning to supply newer info.

column1: What is a hallucination?
column2: Model output that looks plausible but is false, incorrect or made up (e.g. invented citations).

column1: Why do models hallucinate?
column2: They are probabilistic next-token predictors, and post-training (e.g. RLHF) encourages them to give an answer and please the user.

column1: Can hallucinations be eliminated?
column2:
No. They can be significantly reduced/mitigated (grounding, RAG, prompting, human review), but the probability is never zero.

Exam tip: Beware answers saying "guarantee/ensure/eliminate".

column1: What is bias in gen AI?
column2:
Skew in data/models (from human-generated data) that can cause unfair outcomes.

It usually cannot be fully removed - you acknowledge, mitigate and monitor it.

column1: What is "data dependency" as a model limitation?
column2: Foundation model performance depends heavily on training data; any bias or incompleteness seeps into outputs.

column1: What are edge cases (as a model limitation)?
column2:
Rare scenarios with few examples in the training data, where the model performs worse.

Addressed with grounding or fine-tuning.

column1: What are emergent capabilities?
column2: Abilities that foundation models show without having been explicitly trained for them.

column1: Why is non-determinism a challenge for gen AI?
column2: The same prompt can yield different outputs (probabilistic generation), so results are hard to reproduce - testing and evaluation are critical.

column1: What are the four primary types of Machine Learning?
column2:
Machine Learning algorithms are generally categorized by how they learn from data: 
* Supervised Learning
* Unsupervised Learning
* Semi-Supervised Learning
* Reinforcement Learning

column1: What is supervised learning?
column2:
Training on LABELED data (inputs + known outputs) to predict outputs for new unseen inputs (classification, prediction).

Example: 
* spam vs not spam
* house price prediction
* image categorization
Task types:
* Classification
* Regression

column1: What is generalization?
column2: A model's ability to produce accurate outputs for new, unseen data it was not shown during training.

column1: What is unsupervised learning?
column2:
Finding patterns/structure in UNLABELED data.

The model is given unlabeled data without explicitly assigned target outputs. It analyzes the dataset to discover hidden patterns, underlying structures, or natural groupings on its own.

Examples:
* clustering
* grouping customers
* topic discovery
* anomaly detection (e.g. k-means).
Task types:
* Clustering
* Dimensionality Reduction
* Association Rules

column1: What is reinforcement learning?
column2:
An agent learns by interacting with an environment and receiving rewards/penalties (feedback) toward a goal. It learns through trial-and-error using positive and negative feedback rather than fixed ground truth labels.

Examples:
* used in games (AlphaGo)
* robotics
* autonomous vehicles
* recommendations

column1: What is self-supervised learning?
column2: A technique where the model creates its own labels from the data; used in building/training foundation models.

column1: How does semi-supervised learning bridge the gap between supervised and unsupervised?
column2:
It uses a small amount of labeled data combined with a large volume of unlabeled data during training. This significantly reduces the time and cost of manual data annotation while keeping high accuracy.

Examples: 
* medical image analysis (few doctor-labeled X-rays + thousands of unlabeled scans)
* speech recognition

column1: Which learning type fits: classify emails as spam/not spam?
column2: Supervised learning.

column1: Which learning type fits: discover topics in a collection of documents?
column2: Unsupervised learning.

column1: Which learning type fits: AI in a video game gets rewards/penalties for actions?
column2: Reinforcement learning.

column1: Which learning type fits: detect unusual transactions that deviate from the norm?
column2: Unsupervised learning (anomaly detection).

column1: What are the five data quality factors?
column2:
* Accuracy
* Representativeness (inclusive)
* Relevance
* Completeness
* Consistency

column1: What does "garbage in, garbage out" mean?
column2: Output quality is bounded by input data quality. Inaccurate data -> model learns inaccurate patterns.

column1: Data quality factor compromised by factual errors and mislabeled details?
column2: Accuracy.

column1: Data quality factor: data from multiple sources in different formats and labeling?
column2: Consistency.

column1: Data quality factor: data does not reflect the scenarios the model will face (skewed samples)?
column2: Representativeness (and relevance) - leads to biased outcomes.

column1: Is data quality absolute?
column2: No. It is relative to the use case: the same dataset can be high quality for one application and low quality for another.

column1: What are the data accessibility considerations?
column2:
Availability (in development AND production), cost of acquiring/labeling, format the model can process, and non-technical access:
* Permissions
* Authorization
* Licensing
* Ownership

column1: Structured vs unstructured data?
column2:
Structured:
* Tabular/relational data (databases, spreadsheets, CSV).

Unstructured:
* Free text
* Emails
* Images
* Audio
* Video
* PDFs

column1: Which Google Cloud product stores unstructured data?
column2: Cloud Storage (any file type, serverless, highly scalable).

column1: Which Google Cloud products hold structured data?
column2: Cloud SQL, Spanner, AlloyDB (relational), BigQuery (data warehouse), Bigtable, Firestore.

column1: How much time do AI teams typically spend preparing/making data accessible?
column2: Roughly 60-80% of project time.

column1: What are the stages of the ML development lifecycle?
column2:
Gather data → Prepare data → Train model → Deploy & predict → Manage

Management includes:
* Version control
* Performance tracking
* Drift monitoring

column1: What is drift?
column2:
Drift is a change over time in production data, relationships in the data, or model performance that causes quality to degrade.

Main types:
* Data drift - input distribution changes.
* Concept drift - the relationship between inputs and correct outputs changes.
* Prediction drift - model outputs shift.
It is a "when", not an "if".

column1: Drift monitoring vs versioning?
column2:
Drift = changes in the data/performance over time.

Versioning = tracking different versions of the model (v1, v2...).

column1: What is training-serving skew?
column2: A difference between the data distribution (or transformations) used in training and in production.

column1: Open-source/open-weight vs closed models?
column2:
Open models (e.g. Gemma, Llama, Mistral, Qwen, DeepSeek):
* Weights downloadable
* Can be customized and self-hosted.
Closed models (e.g. Gemini):
* Accessed via API/black box.

column1: What is a "black box" in gen AI?
column2: Standard foundation models whose internals we can't access/modify; we interact only through prompts, parameters and APIs.

column1: Why is evaluation a key challenge in gen AI?
column2: Building is easy with modern tools; testing/validating quality continuously (including after every model version change) is the hard part.

column1: What are the four exam domains of the GAIL certification?
column2:
# Fundamentals of gen AI
# Google Cloud's gen AI offerings
# Techniques to improve gen AI model output
# Business strategies for successful gen AI solutions

column1: What is the main goal of the Generative AI Leader certification?
column2: To validate business-level knowledge of generative AI concepts, Google Cloud AI offerings, output-improvement techniques, and responsible AI adoption strategies.

column1: What is Natural Language Processing (NLP)?
column2: A branch of AI that enables computers to understand, interpret, generate, and interact with human language.

column1: How does generative AI differ from traditional discriminative ML?
column2: Generative AI creates new content, while discriminative ML predicts labels, classifications, or values from input data.

column1: What happens during data ingestion?
column2:
Raw data is collected and brought into a system from sources such as:
* Databases
* Files
* APIs
* Streams
* Cloud storage

column1: What happens during data preparation?
column2: Data is cleaned, transformed, labeled, validated, and structured so it can be used effectively for training or inference.

column1: What happens during model training?
column2: A model learns patterns from prepared data by adjusting its internal parameters.

column1: What happens during model deployment?
column2: A trained model is made available for real-world use through an API, application, workflow, or endpoint.

column1: What is the business value of using multiple data types in generative AI?
column2: Multimodal AI can understand richer real-world inputs and produce more useful outputs, such as analyzing documents with images or answering questions using text, charts, and video.

column1: What are the three main ways to make a model use relevant knowledge beyond training?
column2:
Prompt engineering
Grounding (including RAG)
Fine-tuning

column1: In what order should customization approaches be tried?
column2:
Recommended order:
# Prompt engineering - cheapest, plan A.
# Grounding/RAG.
# Fine-tuning - last resort, most expensive.

column1: Why is prompt engineering "plan A"?
column2:
Advantages:
* Cheapest and fastest
* Easy to learn using natural language
* No change to the model
* Skills can be reused when configuring agents

column1: What are the components of a prompt?
column2:
Prompt components:
* Task (mandatory)
* Contextual information/system instructions (optional)
* Examples (optional)

column1: What is zero-shot prompting?
column2: A prompt with only the task and no examples; relies on the model's pre-existing knowledge.

column1: What is one-shot prompting?
column2: Providing exactly one example in the prompt.

column1: What is few-shot prompting?
column2: Providing multiple examples in the prompt so the model learns the pattern/format.

column1: What do examples in a prompt mainly influence?
column2:
Examples mainly guide the model's output format, style, tone, and reasoning pattern, but they can also influence content and task interpretation.

For best results, use examples similar to the real task. Irrelevant examples can reduce quality and waste tokens.

column1: What is the downside of adding many examples?
column2: More tokens = higher cost and latency; poor/irrelevant examples waste resources.

column1: What is role prompting?
column2:
Assigning the model a persona/role (e.g. "You are a customer service agent...") to guide style, tone and focus.

Also specify the target audience.

column1: What is prompt chaining?
column2: A conversation where each prompt builds on the previous response; useful for complex tasks and easier to troubleshoot because a faulty step is easier to find and fix.

column1: What is chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting?
column2:
Guiding the model through intermediate reasoning steps by splitting a complex task into sub-steps.

Improves reasoning, accuracy and explainability; helps with troubleshooting.

column1: What is ReAct?
column2:
Reasoning + Acting: the model reasons (thought), chooses an action/tool, observes the result, then loops again until the goal is met.

Foundation of agent behavior.

column1: CoT vs ReAct?
column2:
CoT (Chain-of-Thought) = internal reasoning over intermediate steps.

ReAct (Reasoning + Acting) = reasoning combined with external actions using tools and a feedback loop.

Often combined.

column1: Task: find the highest-rated restaurant near my current location. CoT or ReAct?
column2: ReAct (needs external tools such as GPS/search).

column1: Task: summarize a long article. CoT or ReAct?
column2: Chain-of-thought (understanding and distilling; no external tool).

column1: What is self-consistency prompting?
column2:
Generate multiple solutions and choose the most consistent one.

Improves reliability but increases cost/latency.

column1: What are prompt templates/variables?
column2:
Parameterized prompts (e.g. {platform}, {audience}) that can be reused with different values.

Promotes reusability.

column1: What does the temperature parameter control?
column2:
Controls randomness/creativity.
* Low (~0) = near-deterministic, factual (legal, financial, medical).
* High = more creative (marketing).

column1: What do top-K and top-P do?
column2:
Limit the pool of candidate next tokens:
* Top-K = the K most probable tokens.
* Top-P (nucleus) = tokens up to a cumulative probability threshold.

column1: What does max output tokens control?
column2: The maximum length of the generated response (also affects cost).

column1: What are safety settings?
column2: Configurable filters that block harmful content (hate speech, dangerous, sexually explicit, harassment) at chosen thresholds.

column1: Do prompt engineering and grounding modify the model?
column2:
No. The model stays frozen.

Only fine-tuning changes the model's weights.

column1: What is grounding?
column2: Connecting a model's output to verifiable external sources (company docs, databases, Google Search) so it can use data it never saw in training.

column1: Why ground a model?
column2: To overcome the knowledge cutoff, use private/internal data, reduce hallucinations and provide citations.

column1: What is RAG?
column2: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG): retrieve relevant information from a knowledge base (via semantic search), augment the prompt with it, and generate a grounded response.

column1: What are the three RAG steps?
column2:
Retrieval: find relevant information in an external source.

Augmentation: add it to the prompt.

Generation: the LLM writes the answer.

column1: Grounding vs RAG?
column2:
Grounding = generic term for connecting to an external source (e.g. Google Search).

RAG = a specific grounding architecture with a retriever + generator over your knowledge base.

column1: What are the benefits of RAG?
column2: More accurate and relevant outputs, reduced hallucinations, citations to sources (explainability), extends the LLM without changing it.

column1: What is the main risk of RAG?
column2:
Garbage in, garbage out: you own the knowledge base, so outdated or inaccurate content produces poor answers.

It must be maintained.

column1: RAG vs a traditional database?
column2:
A traditional database stores and queries structured records, typically through SQL, filters, joins, or keyword/full-text search.

RAG uses semantic search over embeddings to retrieve meaning-relevant content, then adds it to the prompt so the LLM can generate a grounded answer.

column1: What is Google Search grounding?
column2: A configuration that lets Gemini run Google searches for current info beyond its cutoff (e.g. last weekend's scores).

column1: What is fine-tuning?
column2:
Further training a foundation model on your own targeted data to specialize it.

It changes weights and creates a new model you must manage.

column1: When is fine-tuning appropriate?
column2:
When the limitation is NOT solvable with data access:
* Specific behavior
* Internal workflows/policies
* Complex instructions
* Specific output formats or domain tasks
Use it after prompting and grounding are exhausted.

column1: Why is fine-tuning a last resort?
column2:
Disadvantages:
* Expensive and complex
* Needs expertise and time
* Requires ongoing maintenance
* Not every model supports it

column1: Which models can be fine-tuned?
column2: Only models that support fine-tuning - check this when choosing a model.

column1: What is "human in the loop"?
column2: Keeping humans to review, validate, moderate and approve outputs, especially for high-risk decisions, sensitive data and regulated workflows.

column1: Which techniques overcome foundation model limitations?
column2:
* Prompt engineering
* Grounding/RAG
* Fine-tuning
* Human-in-the-loop

column1: What is prompt tuning?
column2: Adapting a model's behavior by learning or optimizing prompt representations rather than fully retraining model weights.

column1: What is prebuilt RAG with Agent Search?
column2: A managed Google Cloud approach that combines enterprise search and retrieval with generative AI so applications can answer from connected data sources.

column1: What is the difference between a prompt and a completion?
column2: A prompt is the input or instruction given to a model; a completion is the model's generated response.

column1: What are RAG APIs?
column2: Google Cloud APIs that let developers add retrieval-augmented generation capabilities to custom applications.

column1: What is an AI guardrail?
column2:
A control that helps prevent unsafe, inaccurate, biased, or non-compliant AI behavior.

Examples:
* Content filters
* Validation rules
* Human review

column1: What is first-party enterprise data grounding?
column2: Grounding responses using an organization's own trusted data, documents, databases, or knowledge bases.

column1: What is third-party data grounding?
column2: Grounding responses using trusted external sources, such as licensed content, partner data, or approved public sources.

column1: What is world-data grounding?
column2: Grounding responses using broad public web information, such as Google Search results.

column1: What are examples of generative AI monitoring practices?
column2:
Key activities:
* Tracking KPIs
* Monitoring quality and latency
* Reviewing outputs
* Managing versions
* Applying updates and security patches
* Detecting data or model drift

column1: What is evaluation in generative AI?
column2:
Systematic testing of model outputs against criteria such as:
* Accuracy
* Relevance
* Safety
* Tone
* Completeness
* Latency
* Cost

column1: What factors should you consider when choosing a model?
column2:
Key model selection criteria:
* Modality
* Context window
* Security
* Availability and reliability
* Cost
* Performance
* Fine-tuning/customization support
* Ease of integration

column1: Gemini Pro vs Flash / Flash-Lite?
column2:
Pro models are intended for complex reasoning and higher-quality tasks, usually with higher latency and cost.

Flash and Flash-Lite prioritize low latency and low cost, making them suitable for high-volume chatbots, classification, summarization, and simple generation.

Choose the cheapest model that meets the required quality, latency, and cost constraints.

column1: How should you pick the model size?
column2:
Pick the smallest, cheapest model that meets requirements.

Never use the biggest "just in case".

column1: Best practice to optimize model cost during development?
column2:
First prove feasibility with the most powerful model, then downgrade versions/tiers until quality is no longer acceptable.

Keep the cheapest model that works.

column1: Why is output cost higher than input cost?
column2: Output involves generation compute (processing time), so output tokens are priced higher than input tokens.

column1: What cost components exist for gen AI solutions?
column2:
Main cost categories:
* Training (only when building/fine-tuning)
* Deployment (infrastructure)
* Usage (tokens, requests, etc.)

column1: What pricing metrics exist for models/APIs?
column2:
Pricing models may include:
* Tokens (foundation models)
* Characters (e.g. Translation API)
* Number of requests
* Compute time
* Subscriptions
* Licensing fees
* Free tiers

column1: What tool helps estimate Google Cloud costs?
column2: Google Cloud Pricing Calculator (needs rough volume estimates).

column1: Trade-off of heavy customization?
column2:
More effort to build and maintain (support, performance, cost).

Customize only when needed; reuse pre-built solutions where possible.

column1: What factors determine solution needs/scale?
column2:
Key considerations:
* Target audience (internal vs public)
* Usage frequency
* Customization needed
* Latency tolerance
* Accuracy tolerance
* Privacy/security/compliance
* Explainability
* Connectivity
* Time, people and budget

column1: How should you define latency and accuracy requirements?
column2:
Realistically, define acceptable ranges (error budget); "perfect" is unaffordable.

Lower latency may require smaller models.

column1: Why does a security requirement influence model/platform choice?
column2:
Sensitive data (PII, payment, health) and regulated industries require:
* Encryption
* Access control
* Compliance
* Enterprise-grade protections

column1: What is the single entry point for AI on Google Cloud?
column2: The Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform (formerly Vertex AI; renamed April 2026) - a fully managed, unified AI development platform.

column1: What is Model Garden?
column2:
A central hub in the platform to discover, customize and deploy 200+ models:
* Google first-party models
* Partner/closed models (e.g. Anthropic Claude)
* Open models (Gemma, Llama, Mistral, Qwen, DeepSeek)

column1: What is Gemini?
column2: Google's flagship family of multimodal foundation models (closed source).

column1: What is Gemma?
column2: Google's open-source/open-weight model family; can be downloaded and run locally, on premises or on Google Cloud.

column1: What is Nano Banana?
column2: Commercial name of a Gemini-based model specialized in high-quality image generation/editing.

column1: What is Veo?
column2: Google's video generation model.

column1: What is Lyria?
column2: Google's music generation model.

column1: What is Chirp?
column2: Google's audio/speech model (e.g. speech-to-text).

column1: What is Gemini Nano?
column2:
A lightweight, on-device (edge) version of Gemini that runs on Pixel/Android devices.

Advantages:
* Offline
* Private
* Fast
Not the same as Nano Banana.

column1: What are Google's pre-built AI APIs?
column2:
Google Cloud services and APIs:
* Speech-to-Text
* Text-to-Speech
* Translation
* Document Translation
* Document AI
* Cloud Vision
* Video Intelligence
* Natural Language API

column1: Pre-built API pros and cons?
column2:
Pros:
* Fast
* Simple
* No ML expertise required
* Quick to embed
Cons:
* Single narrow function
* Trained/maintained by Google
* Generic - may not be specific enough to your domain

column1: Which API analyzes sentiment and categorizes text?
column2: Cloud Natural Language API.

column1: Which API extracts data from documents like invoices/contracts?
column2: Document AI.

column1: Which API translates while preserving PDF layout?
column2: Document Translation API.

column1: What is Agent Studio vs Google AI Studio?
column2:
Agent Studio (Google Cloud console/Agent Platform):
* Enterprise-grade
* Designed for professionals and large projects
Google AI Studio:
* Free and simple
* Designed for individuals, beginners and experimentation
* Doesn't accept corporate Workspace accounts
* Data may be used under different terms

column1: What tools exist in the Agent Platform for the ML lifecycle?
column2:
Available capabilities and tools:
* Feature Store
* Model Registry
* Experiments
* Metadata management
* Evaluation
* Pipelines
* Model Monitoring
* Endpoints/batch deployment
* Tuning
* RAG Engine
* Vector Search

column1: What does Feature Store do?
column2: Central repository to share, serve and reuse features consistently between training and production.

column1: What does Model Registry do?
column2: Manages model versions, tracks changes and organizes models through their life cycle.

column1: What does Experiments/Metadata do?
column2: Tracks experiments, evaluation metrics and artifacts across trained model versions.

column1: What do Pipelines do?
column2:
Automate and orchestrate the end-to-end ML workflow:
* Data preparation
* Training
* Evaluation
* Deployment

column1: What does Model Monitoring do?
column2: Detects performance degradation, input skew and drift; can trigger updates or retraining.

column1: Which tool: track versions and record of changes?
column2: Model Registry.

column1: Which tool: find cause of declining production performance?
column2: Model Monitoring.

column1: Which tool: automate the entire ML pipeline from data prep to deployment?
column2: Pipelines (workflow orchestration).

column1: Which tool: label data, experiment with architectures and deploy models?
column2: The platform layer - Agent Platform.

column1: What is Gemini app?
column2: Google's consumer/commercial chatbot (web/mobile) powered by Gemini; can use Google Search.

column1: What is Google Workspace with Gemini?
column2:
Gemini embedded in Gmail, Docs, Slides, Sheets, Meet, Drive, etc. via a side panel.

Capabilities:
* Write
* Summarize
* Analyze
* Generate images
* Provide live translated captions
An admin enables or disables features.

column1: What do Google Vids and AppSheet do?
column2:
Vids: AI video creation/editing.

AppSheet: no-code app development.

column1: What is Gemini Notebook (formerly NotebookLM)?
column2:
A personalized AI research assistant grounded ONLY in the sources you upload.

Features:
* Isolated, hyper-focused environment with citations
* Audio overviews
* Slide decks
* Quizzes
* Mind maps
* Reports

column1: Gemini Notebook source behavior?
column2:
Limitations:
* Sources are COPIED, not linked, so you must manually re-sync changes.
* Outputs are read-only.
* Chat history isn't kept long (save to note).
* No Google Search.
* Data isn't used to train models.

column1: What does "chat-only" sharing in Gemini Notebook do?
column2: Lets viewers query the notebook without seeing the underlying source files.

column1: What is Gemini Enterprise?
column2:
A subscription-based single point of entry app to build/use AI agents grounded in company data from many sources.

Features:
* Connectors
* Google Search/Maps
* Deep research
* Agent marketplace
* No-code
Gemini Notebook is part of it.

column1: Gemini Enterprise vs Gemini Notebook?
column2:
Notebook:
* Isolated to chosen sources only
* No external connectivity
Enterprise:
* Connects to external resources via connectors/tools and agents
* Can search Google and company data

column1: Primary purpose of Gemini Enterprise?
column2:
A centralized platform to access AI agents that use company data to assist employees.

NOT a new repository that copies all company data.

column1: What is Gemini for Google Cloud (Cloud Assist)?
column2:
AI assistant embedded in Google Cloud products.

Capabilities:
* Troubleshooting
* Root cause analysis
* Optimization recommendations (security, cost)
* Designing and operating apps

column1: What is Gemini Code Assist?
column2:
AI pair programmer in IDEs.

Capabilities:
* Code suggestions and generation
* Explanations
* Tests
* Documentation
Supports 20+ languages. Best for developer efficiency and collaboration.

column1: What does Gemini in BigQuery/Looker do?
column2:
Writes/explains SQL and generates insights (BigQuery).

Also provides natural-language analytics in Looker (BI platform with separate credentials/licensing).

column1: What do Colab Enterprise and Workbench provide?
column2: Managed Jupyter notebook environments combining text and code for data science and ML.

column1: Gemini in security?
column2:
Helps summarize threats, assess security posture and analyze attack paths.

Customer prompts/responses are not used for training.

column1: What are AI Applications?
column2:
No-code/low-code builders for:
* Search (search & assistant, custom search, healthcare, commerce, media)
* Conversational agents
* Recommendations
Connected to data stores.

column1: Which product for recommendations without coding?
column2: AI Applications (recommendations/search).

column1: What are data stores in AI Applications?
column2:
Structured and unstructured knowledge bases (Cloud Storage, BigQuery, websites, etc.) that agents use for grounding.

Indexing can take minutes to hours.

column1: Agent Search capabilities?
column2:
Search over organization data with:
* Summaries
* Citations
* Follow-ups
Industry tuning (retail, media, healthcare) reduces hallucinations via grounding.

column1: Conversational Agents (CX): flows vs playbooks?
column2:
Flows = deterministic, predefined pages/rules.

Playbooks = generative, natural-language-driven.

Hybrid = combines both.

column1: What are Customer Experience Agent Studio, Agent Assist and Insights?
column2:
CX Agent Studio: design/build chatbots and voicebots (full automation).

Agent Assist: suggestions, transcription and summaries for live human agents (augmentation).

Insights: analytics on interactions and performance.

column1: Which product helps human call-center agents during live calls?
column2: Agent Assist (improves efficiency, consistency, first-call resolution).

column1: Which product designs chatbots/voicebots that understand user intent?
column2: Conversational Agents / CX Agent Studio.

column1: Which product analyzes conversation FAQs and effectiveness?
column2: Conversational Insights.

column1: What is a "symbol" company in exam questions?
column2: A fictional company (Symbol Retail, Symbol Banking...) used to frame realistic scenario questions.

column1: What is AutoML?
column2: A Vertex AI capability that automates parts of the ML workflow, such as training and tuning models, so users can build models with less manual ML expertise.

column1: What is Contact Center as a Service (CCaaS)?
column2:
A cloud-based contact-center platform that can integrate AI capabilities such as:
* Virtual agents
* Agent assist
* Conversation analytics

column1: Which Google Cloud service is commonly used for data ingestion and storage?
column2: Google Cloud Storage, BigQuery, Pub/Sub and Dataflow are commonly used depending on the data type and workload.

column1: Which Google Cloud service is commonly used to prepare and transform data?
column2: Dataprep, Dataflow, Dataproc and BigQuery can be used for data preparation and transformation.

column1: What is Agent Search?
column2: A managed search service that provides enterprise search and retrieval across websites, documents and structured data, often used for RAG.

column1: What are the layers of the gen AI landscape?
column2:
From bottom to top:
* Infrastructure
* Platform
* Models
* Agents
* Gen AI applications

column1: What does the gen AI application layer do?
column2: User-facing front end (website, mobile app, API, chatbot) through which users or other services interact.

column1: What does the infrastructure layer include?
column2: Compute (CPUs, GPUs, TPUs), storage, networking and security.

column1: GPU vs TPU?
column2:
GPU (Graphics Processing Unit):
* General-purpose parallel accelerator originally designed for graphics
* Widely used for ML training and inference
* Nvidia is one major vendor
TPU (Tensor Processing Unit):
* Google's custom ASIC
* Optimized specifically for tensor/ML workloads
* Available through Google Cloud

column1: What is a hypercomputer?
column2: Google's cluster-computing approach aggregating many GPUs/TPUs to scale training and serving of massive models.

column1: Why manage compute and storage independently in the cloud?
column2:
Virtualization lets you scale each separately; networking connects them.

Bandwidth/latency can become the bottleneck.

column1: IaaS vs fully managed vs serverless?
column2:
IaaS (e.g. VMs): you configure resources.

Fully managed (Agent Platform): you configure, platform operates.

Serverless (BigQuery, Cloud Run): no infrastructure to configure.

column1: Why use the cloud for gen AI?
column2:
Advantages:
* Pay per use
* No big upfront hardware investment
* Easy to experiment/prototype/proof of concept
* Automatic scaling and maintenance

column1: What are on-premises, hybrid and multicloud?
column2:
On-prem = own data center.

Hybrid = cloud + on-prem.

Multicloud = multiple cloud providers.

column1: What is edge computing and when is it used?
column2:
Running AI on devices/servers close to the data source.

Use when:
* Connectivity is limited/unreliable
* Real-time response is required
* Data privacy forbids moving data to cloud
* Offline use is needed

column1: Edge or cloud: medical device giving real-time feedback during surgery?
column2: Edge.

column1: Edge or cloud: chatbot handling millions of daily e-commerce inquiries?
column2: Cloud (scale and capacity).

column1: Edge or cloud: smart-city traffic analysis with large data volumes?
column2: Cloud (centralized processing capacity).

column1: Steps to deploy models at the edge?
column2: Convert the model to a lightweight version, package it with dependencies in a container, deploy, then manage/monitor and sync back with the backend.

column1: Which Google Cloud services handle messaging, SQL, storage, data warehouse?
column2: Pub/Sub (messaging, near real time), Cloud SQL/Spanner (relational), Cloud Storage (objects), BigQuery (data warehouse).

column1: What is Cloud Run vs Cloud Run functions?
column2:
Cloud Run = serverless containers for long-running services (e.g. websites, front ends).

Cloud Run functions = small event-driven code triggered by events (e.g. file upload) and auto-scaled.

column1: Why does exam say "near real time" rather than "real time"?
column2: Gen AI workflows typically operate in streaming/near-real-time (seconds), not millisecond real time.

column1: What does IAM do on Google Cloud?
column2:
IAM controls authorization: it determines which authenticated principals (users, groups, service accounts) can access which Google Cloud resources and what actions they can perform, through IAM roles and policy bindings.

Authentication verifies identity; IAM then decides permissions.

column1: Authentication vs authorization?
column2:
Authentication = who you are.

Authorization = what you're allowed to do.

column1: What is the principle of least privilege?
column2: Grant only the minimum permissions needed, and review them regularly.

column1: What is zero trust?
column2: Never trust implicitly: every connection between services/users must be authenticated and authorized, with no trusted "perimeter".

column1: Why use an API key?
column2:
To authenticate calls from an application to an API (e.g. Gemini API).

Keys should be administered and rotated, not created freely by every user.

column1: What does Sensitive Data Protection do?
column2:
Detects sensitive data (PII) and de-identifies it:
* Mask
* Redact
* Tokenize/pseudonymize

column1: What is PII?
column2: Personally Identifiable Information - any data that can identify an individual; must be protected.

column1: Encryption on Google Cloud?
column2:
Data at rest is encrypted automatically by Google (cannot be disabled).

You can optionally manage keys with CMEK for compliance.

column1: What is Google's Secure AI Framework (SAIF)?
column2: A framework of guidelines/best practices (not a product) to build and deploy AI securely and address AI-specific threats.

column1: What are Mandiant and Security Command Center?
column2:
Mandiant = threat intelligence/consulting for proactive security.

Security Command Center = dashboard for security posture and findings.

column1: How to secure the ML lifecycle?
column2:
Key practices:
* Protect and validate data
* Anonymize sensitive data
* Control access to training data/model
* Verify pre-built models
* Monitor for tampering/anomalies
* Update regularly
* Review permissions

column1: What is an adversarial attack/test?
column2:
A model or actor attacking/testing another model.

Malicious use must be prevented, but red-team-style adversarial testing is a useful evaluation technique (costs more).

column1: What does the Observability suite include?
column2:
* Logging
* Monitoring
* Error reporting
* Tracing

column1: What is a prompt injection attack?
column2: An attack where malicious input tries to override a model's instructions or cause it to reveal data, bypass controls, or take unintended actions.

column1: How can organizations reduce prompt-injection risk?
column2:
Mitigation methods:
* Validate inputs
* Restrict tool permissions
* Separate instructions from untrusted content
* Use guardrails
* Monitor behavior
* Apply least-privilege access

column1: What is data exfiltration in AI systems?
column2: Unauthorized transfer or leakage of sensitive data from an organization through an AI system or its integrations.

column1: What is data anonymization?
column2: Removing or altering identifying information so individuals cannot reasonably be identified.

column1: What is pseudonymization?
column2: Replacing identifying information with pseudonyms or tokens, where re-identification may still be possible using additional information.

column1: What is an AI agent?
column2: Software that tries to achieve a goal by observing the world and acting on it with available tools, powered by a foundation model, with autonomy.

column1: What are the core components of a gen AI agent?
column2:
Core components:
* Foundation model (brain / NLU)
* Tools (hands)
* Reasoning loop/orchestration (guided by prompts)
* Memory/data

column1: What is the reasoning loop?
column2:
Iterative cycle:
# Observe
# Reason/plan
# Decide
# Act with a tool
# Observe the result
# Repeat until the goal is achieved

column1: What distinguishes an agent from a standalone LLM?
column2: Reasoning loop (e.g. ReAct) plus the ability to call tools to take actions and manage multi-step tasks.

column1: How is an agent's behavior configured?
column2: With natural-language prompt engineering (role, instructions, examples) - no code needed in managed environments.

column1: What tool types do agents use?
column2:
* Extensions (connect to APIs)
* Functions (reusable specialized actions)
* Data stores (grounding/RAG)
* Plugins (new skills/integrations)

column1: Which tool type connects an agent to external services via APIs?
column2: Extensions.

column1: Which tool type defines specific reusable actions?
column2: Functions.

column1: Which tool type gives access to up-to-date or private information?
column2: Data stores.

column1: What is an API?
column2: Application Programming Interface - the standard way software systems communicate.

column1: What is MCP?
column2: Model Context Protocol - open (de facto standard) protocol that lets agents connect to tools/data sources in a consistent way.

column1: What is A2A?
column2: Agent-to-Agent protocol - open protocol for agents communicating with each other.

column1: Conversational vs workflow agents?
column2:
Conversational:
* Chat/voice Q&A
* Simpler, directly user-facing
* Failures are noticed quickly
Workflow:
* Multi-step process automation (onboarding, order fulfillment, research)
* Often multi-agent

column1: Customer onboarding with multiple steps: which agent type?
column2: Workflow agent.

column1: Why do conversational agents need extra care?
column2: They face paying customers directly, so problems are noticed immediately and hurt customer satisfaction.

column1: Deterministic vs generative agents?
column2:
* Deterministic = predefined paths, predictable, same input → same output.
* Generative = LLM-driven, flexible, natural language, but non-deterministic.
* Hybrid = combines control with flexibility.

column1: Why keep agents simple and use multi-agent systems?
column2:
Borrowed from microservices: simple agents are faster, easier to troubleshoot, scalable and flexible.

Complex goals are split into sub-goals handled by collaborating agents.

column1: How do agents relate to gen AI applications?
column2: Agents are intelligent components inside a larger application that provides the UI and overall goals.

column1: Which Google Cloud service runs agent workflows?
column2: Agent Platform (managed), or Cloud Run / Cloud Run functions for custom deployments.

column1: How do you choose a way to build agents?
column2:
Balance effort/expertise versus control/flexibility:
* No-code (AI Applications, Gemini Enterprise)
* Custom code on the platform

column1: What should drive a gen AI initiative?
column2: Business value (revenue, cost, satisfaction, KPIs) - start from the problem, not the technology.

column1: What is solutionism?
column2:
Having a solution (gen AI) without a problem.

Avoid it by defining needs first and then evaluating tools.

column1: What is the best way to implement gen AI strategy?
column2:
Both approaches together:
* Top-down: vision, budget, priorities
* Bottom-up: experimentation, pain points, sharing

column1: Why involve mid-level managers and individual contributors?
column2: They are closest to the workflows and best at identifying pain points and bottlenecks.

column1: What is the executive/top-down role?
column2: Set a clear vision aligned with strategy, prioritize use cases, allocate budget, drive responsible AI governance and communication.

column1: How to choose the first use case?
column2:
Low-risk but meaningful:
* Not mission-critical (avoid disruption)
* Not trivial (so impact is visible)
Prioritize actionable, affordable, high-ROI cases.

column1: What does the "fail fast" culture mean?
column2: Encourage experimentation on a small scale, learn from failures quickly and share lessons.

column1: What is an MVP and why use it?
column2: Minimum viable product (MVP): good enough to deploy, then improved iteratively using real user feedback, avoiding endless development.

column1: Augmentation vs automation?
column2:
Augmentation = AI assists humans (human decides).

Automation = AI performs the task end to end.

Augmentation is often a first step before automation.

column1: Which tasks suit automation?
column2:
Repetitive, rule-based, time-consuming tasks.

Examples:
* FAQ answering
* Data entry
* Product descriptions
* Formatting

column1: Which tasks suit augmentation?
column2:
Tasks requiring human judgment, creativity, relationship-building, strategic thinking, or handling high-risk decisions.

Example: a financial advisor using AI analysis.

column1: Why keep humans in the loop?
column2:
Key areas requiring human oversight:
* Data selection
* Output evaluation
* Monitoring
* High-risk decisions
* Sensitive and regulated workflows

column1: What are the principles of responsible AI?
column2:
Key responsible AI principles:
* Transparency
* Privacy
* Data quality
* Bias and fairness
* Accountability and explainability
* Security and safety

column1: What is explainability/interpretability?
column2:
Explainability/interpretability means understanding why a model produced a particular output.

It is especially important in regulated or high-stakes domains, such as:
* Finance
* Healthcare
* Government
Decisions may need to be justified, audited, or challenged.

column1: What must be done about bias and fairness?
column2:
Ways to mitigate bias:
* Use diverse and representative training data
* Regularly audit model performance
* Mitigate bias in downstream applications
* Continuously monitor results

column1: Which loan-assessment steps support ethical AI?
column2: Use diverse, representative data and regularly audit model performance to detect emerging bias.

column1: What legal topics apply to gen AI?
column2:
Key legal and compliance risks:
* Data privacy
* Non-discrimination
* Intellectual property and copyright
* Product liability
* Regulatory compliance

column1: Why use Gemini for images instead of copying from the web?
column2:
Generating images with Gemini can reduce the risk of using unlicensed or copyrighted material copied from the web.

However, it does not eliminate all risks related to:
* Intellectual property
* Trademarks
* Likeness rights
* Licensing
Review usage rights and organizational policies before publishing.

column1: Key steps for planning for impact?
column2:
A continuous improvement process:
* Define key metrics/KPIs
* Collect and analyze data
* Iterate and improve

column1: What is the lab-to-production gap?
column2:
A model that performs well in lab or leaderboard evaluations may not deliver the same value in production.

Therefore:
* Evaluate it on your own use cases
* Track business KPIs

column1: Why track KPIs for gen AI?
column2:
To demonstrate tangible value and ROI, justify continued investment, and measure improvements in:
* Customer satisfaction
* Efficiency
* Productivity

column1: How often should models be evaluated or retrained?
column2:
Evaluate models continuously but cost-consciously.

Recommended practices:
* Establish a regular evaluation cadence
* Retrain only when needed, e.g. when drift is detected
* Re-test after every model version change

column1: What is error budget?
column2:
The amount of errors or incidents that can be tolerated without negatively affecting user experience.

In Site Reliability Engineering (SRE), acceptable ranges should be explicitly defined.

column1: Why do exam answers with "guarantee/ensure" tend to be wrong?
column2:
Generative AI cannot guarantee accuracy, security, or zero hallucinations.

Use realistic terms such as:
* Reduce
* Mitigate
* Improve
Avoid claims of complete elimination or guaranteed accuracy.

column1: What are key benefits of using Google Cloud for gen AI?
column2:
Benefits of using managed AI platforms:
* Access to pre-trained models, such as Gemini
* Automatic upgrades and security patches
* Enterprise-grade security and compliance
* Scalable infrastructure
* Ability to experiment without starting from scratch

column1: Does Google Cloud provide ready-made gen AI solutions for every domain?
column2: Not fully. Industry-specific AI solutions for retail, healthcare, media, and other sectors are growing, but universal solutions are not yet available for every use case.

column1: How should organizations build capability for gen AI?
column2:
Key steps for building AI capabilities:
* Invest in training and talent
* Encourage collaboration and knowledge sharing
* Drive organizational change
* Stay informed about developments

column1: Why continuously evaluate when new model versions are released?
column2:
New model versions may change behavior, features, and costs.

Therefore:
* Re-test prompts
* Re-validate outputs
* Re-evaluate performance after every update

column1: What is A/B testing in generative AI?
column2: A/B testing compares two or more model versions, prompts, or user experiences to determine which performs better against defined metrics.

column1: What is change management in AI adoption?
column2:
Preparing people, processes, and culture for AI-driven changes through:
* Communication
* Training
* Support
* Governance
* Clear ownership

column1: What is an AI center of excellence?
column2: A centralized team or function that provides AI standards, governance, expertise, reusable assets, and support across an organization.
